A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Action-Sufficient Goal Representations. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original oracle-subgoal evaluations, Discrete Cube simulations and information calculations, and OGBench cube experiments in Figures 1 and 3 and Tables 1, 2, and 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds scene and pixel-based evaluations, autoencoder and Q-based comparisons, and high-level prediction measurements.

M1.justification: The proposed actor-based encoder remains jointly trained with the low-level policy through NLL/AWR, with high-level predicted representations used at deployment. The flow-policy variant already appears in v1. The newly evaluated autoencoder and Q-based encoders are comparison methods.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Discrete Cube and state-based cube manipulation under play/noisy conditions. v2 retains these and adds scene-play and pixel-input visual-cube and visual-scene evaluations in Tables 1, 2, and 5, substantially extending environment and observation-modality coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds an autoencoder representation to the retained raw-goal/value/actor comparison. Appendix I and Table 6 introduce a TD-trained Q-function representation against the actor representation. These add substantively different reconstruction-based and action-conditioned comparison objectives on cube-double-play and cube-triple-play; the existing benchmark algorithms remain.

E3.justification: New Appendix J evaluates high-level predictions along oracle trajectories using squared L2 error against encoded k-step subgoals. Existing cube protocols remain unchanged, including 2.5 million gradient steps, evaluations every 500,000 steps, and 100 trials across five goals. The principal protocol addition is this targeted prediction diagnostic.

E4.justification: v2 adds controls testing whether reconstruction-based compression or Q-learning provides effective goal representations. Appendix J additionally tests whether actor representations burden high-level subgoal prediction, a concern previously discussed without direct measurement. The original raw-goal ablation and Discrete Cube analysis are retained.

E5.justification: The original eight-seed cube results and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting remain. v2 specifies three seeds for visual tasks and four seeds for the Q comparison and prediction analysis. These are additional run-count disclosures for new comparisons, without evidence of increased runs for retained results or new significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Matched cube means and standard deviations are unchanged, but substantial results are added. HIQL actor/value success is 0.78/0.56 on scene-play and 0.53/0.05 and 0.53/0.23 on the visual tasks. However, Table 5 reports H-Flow actor/value reversals of 0.01/0.07 and 0.07/0.19 on those visual tasks. Tables 3, 6, and 7 add autoencoder scores, Q-versus-actor scores of 0.42/0.42 and 0.32/0.41, and lower actor high-level prediction errors.

T1.justification: New Appendix I defines Q-sufficiency, introduces a uniform-optimal-policy assumption, and presents Proposition I.3 and its proof claiming that Q-sufficiency implies action sufficiency. This substantially extends the formal framework. The original KL decomposition, value-sufficiency analysis, and actor excess-NLL bound and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract changes its description of actor representations from action-sufficient to approximately action-sufficient, aligning the summary with the bound already present in v1. The central claims about value sufficiency failing to ensure action sufficiency and the benefits of actor-derived representations remain.

C2.justification: Appendix I now interprets Q-learning as another route to action-sufficient representations, broadening the discussion beyond actor objectives. Section 9 explains autoencoder limitations through retained nuisance information. Appendix J interprets action sufficiency and high-level predictability as compatible in the tested settings, while explicitly qualifying generalization through latent geometry and architectural dependence.

D1.justification: v2 adds project and code access links on its first page. It also describes the autoencoder reconstruction setup and the Q encoder's joint TD training followed by freezing. The original cube hyperparameter table and detailed Discrete Cube specification are retained.

R1.justification: The rewritten related work adds substantial coverage of action-aware representations, including Ghosh et al., Huang et al., and inverse-dynamics studies, while reducing the earlier graph-planning survey. It replaces v1's explicit contradiction claim concerning Park et al. (2025d) with positioning around a missing action-oriented rationale and a scoped novelty claim for hierarchical goal interfaces. Appendix I adds Q-representation positioning.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, preliminaries, motivation, and experimental narrative. Related work moves from Appendix B to Section 2 and is reorganized; limitations are integrated into Concluding Remarks, and full results become part of Experimental Details. Running headers and affiliations are updated, and impact and acknowledgment sections are added.

P2.justification: v2 adds separate pixel-result, Q-comparison, and prediction-loss tables, expands the main comparison and representation-ablation tables, and transposes and expands the full-results table from v1 Table 4 to v2 Table 5. Figures 1–3 retain their substantive plotted content, with caption and placement adjustments.

improvement.justification: Broader evaluation, stronger comparison methods, and the high-level prediction diagnostic address important gaps in v1. However, v2's consistent-improvement narrative conflicts with the H-Flow visual reversals in Table 5. The new Q-sufficiency proof also has a substantive gap: Equation 33 constrains Q almost surely under optimal-action sampling, whereas Equation 35 requires reconstruction across all actions to identify the argmax set. The empirical and positioning gains coexist with these new reporting and theoretical reliability problems, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
